coredata.dc:description: In this study, jellyfish-derived biopolymers were incorporated into polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) matrices to fabricate novel electrospun nanofiber supports (JF-NanoMats) for laccase immobilization. Four nanofiber formulations (PVA, PVA/JF5, PVA/JF25, and PVA/JF50) were synthesized and characterized via FTIR, SEM, TGA, and DSC analyses. The FTIR spectra confirmed the presence of protein-related functional groups in JF-containing nanofibers and revealed spectral shifts indicative of intermolecular interactions between PVA and jellyfish biopolymers. Among the composites, PVA/JF25 displayed superior morphological and thermal properties, including higher porosity and stability, rendering it the most effective support for enzyme immobilization. Laccase was immobilized on nanofiber mats using a standardized protocol to ensure experimental consistency across all samples. Comparative BPA degradation experiments were then performed under identical reaction conditions (pH 4.5, 35 °C), matching the optimal catalytic environment for free laccase. Results demonstrated that all immobilized systems significantly outperformed the free enzyme in terms of degradation efficiency, substrate tolerance, and operational stability. Specifically, the PVA/JF25 system achieved complete BPA removal (100 %) within 120 min and retained over 50 % of its activity after 10 reuse cycles. This study presents an eco-friendly approach for valorizing jellyfish biomass into functional biopolymeric supports and offers a promising strategy for developing high-performance, recyclable nanofiber-based biocatalysts for environmental remediation applications.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: In this study, jellyfish-derived biopolymers were incorporated into polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) matrices to fabricate novel electrospun nanofiber supports (JF-NanoMats) for laccase immobilization. Four nanofiber formulations (PVA, PVA/JF5, PVA/JF25, and PVA/JF50) were synthesized and characterized via FTIR, SEM, TGA, and DSC analyses. The FTIR spectra confirmed the presence of protein-related functional groups in JF-containing nanofibers and revealed spectral shifts indicative of intermolecular interactions between PVA and jellyfish biopolymers. Among the composites, PVA/JF25 displayed superior morphological and thermal properties, including higher porosity and stability, rendering it the most effective support for enzyme immobilization. Laccase was immobilized on nanofiber mats using a standardized protocol to ensure experimental consistency across all samples. Comparative BPA degradation experiments were then performed under identical reaction conditions (pH 4.5, 35 °C), matching the optimal catalytic environment for free laccase. Results demonstrated that all immobilized systems significantly outperformed the free enzyme in terms of degradation efficiency, substrate tolerance, and operational stability. Specifically, the PVA/JF25 system achieved complete BPA removal (100 %) within 120 min and retained over 50 % of its activity after 10 reuse cycles. This study presents an eco-friendly approach for valorizing jellyfish biomass into functional biopolymeric supports and offers a promising strategy for developing high-performance, recyclable nanofiber-based biocatalysts for environmental remediation applications.

ce:section.ce:para: Phenolic compounds are a major class of environmental pollutants commonly found in industrial effluents originating from petrochemical, plastic, pesticide, and pharmaceutical industries. These compounds are toxic, resistant to biodegradation, and can accumulate in the environment, posing serious threats to aquatic ecosystems and human health [1–3]. Among them, bisphenol A (BPA), a synthetic monomer widely used in the production of polycarbonate plastics and epoxy resins, has been classified as an endocrine-disrupting chemical due to its estrogen-mimicking activity [4,5]. BPA exposure has been linked to hormonal imbalances, reproductive disorders, and developmental toxicity, leading to increased regulatory pressure and demand for effective removal strategies from wastewater streams [6,7].

Conventional methods for BPA removal include adsorption, photocatalysis, membrane filtration, and chemical oxidation. While these techniques can achieve high removal efficiencies, they may also present drawbacks such as the potential generation of secondary pollutants and limited substrate specificity in some cases. Although certain photocatalytic systems especially those relying on UV light can be energy-intensive, recent advancements have led to the development of visible-light-driven photocatalysts, which are more energy-efficient and environmentally sustainable [8,9]. In addition to these conventional approaches, recent studies have explored advanced water purification strategies. Aerobic granular sludge (AGS)-based membrane bioreactors have shown improved nutrient removal and reduced fouling through scouring effects [10,11]. Similarly, multifunctional granular materials and biomimetic dynamic membranes integrating adsorption, enzymatic degradation, and membrane separation have demonstrated promising pollutant removal efficiencies [12,13]. While these approaches highlight notable progress, limitations such as high material demand and substrate selectivity remain, underscoring the complementary potential of eco-friendly enzymatic degradation strategies. In contrast, enzymatic degradation has emerged as a promising green alternative due to its mild reaction conditions, high substrate specificity, and minimal formation of harmful byproducts. Particularly, oxidative enzymes such as laccases have demonstrated the ability to break down phenolic structures, including BPA, through radical-mediated oxidation mechanisms. However, one of the challenges in enzymatic applications remains the operational stability of the enzymes under varying environmental conditions. [14–16].

Laccase (EC 1.10.3.2) is a multi‑copper oxidase capable of catalyzing the oxidation of a wide range of phenolic and aromatic compounds using molecular oxygen as the sole electron acceptor. Its broad substrate range, no requirement for additional cofactors, and applicability in pollutant degradation make it a highly attractive biocatalyst for environmental applications [16–18]. However, the free form of laccase is often unstable, sensitive to pH and temperature fluctuations, and difficult to reuse in continuous processes, which limits its industrial applicability [19,20].

To overcome these limitations, enzyme immobilization strategies have been developed to enhance the operational stability, reusability, and activity retention of laccase [21]. Among various support materials, electrospun nanofibers have gained prominence due to their large surface area, high porosity, ease of surface modification, and tunable physical properties [22,23]. These features allow for efficient enzyme loading and diffusion, making nanofiber mats ideal for biocatalytic applications such as wastewater treatment [24,25]. Other immobilization platforms such as polymeric beads, membranes, and hydrogels have also been widely investigated for enzyme stabilization [26–28]. However, these systems often suffer from drawbacks such as limited surface area, diffusion constraints, or reduced mechanical robustness. In contrast, electrospun nanofiber mats provide a highly porous and flexible architecture with large surface-to-volume ratios, enabling more efficient enzyme loading and mass transfer. These features make them particularly attractive for biocatalytic applications, including pollutant removal in wastewater treatment.

Jellyfish (JF) can reproduce excessively at certain times and have negative effects on ecosystem functioning (they directly affect fish populations by consuming fish eggs and larvae, and indirectly affect fish populations by consuming zooplankton, causing mucilage formation) and human health (they cause pain, ache, burning, itching, redness, edema, and blister formation when they come into contact, negatively affecting holidaymakers), but they only limited evaluated as Asian food commercially [29–31]. JF biopolymers are rich in collagen-like proteins and possess unique gel-forming and hydrophilic properties that can enhance matrix interactions when blended with synthetic polymers [32,33]. In recent years, marine-derived biopolymers, particularly those extracted from JF, have attracted attention as sustainable and biodegradable materials for various bioengineering applications [34,35]. For example, JF biomass was used to fabricate electrospun core shell nanofibers loaded with in situ synthesized silver nanoparticles, yielding biocompatible and biodegradable wound dressings with potent antibacterial activity and enhanced healing in preclinical models [36]. Similarly, collagen extracted from Persian Gulf JF was incorporated into electrospun nanofibers to achieve sustained drug release (phenytoin) for improved wound healing and cell compatibility [37]. Beyond wound management, JF-based biohydrogels have been transformed into robust, water-stable ionic cables with superior ionic conductivity for nanofluidic and membrane separation applications [38]. In soft tissue engineering, organic–inorganic biohybrid films combining JF collagen with keratin, silica, and boron have demonstrated pro-angiogenic properties, promoting vascularization in tissue constructs [39]. Moreover, JF nematocyst venom proteins have been utilized as a biotemplate for the biosynthesis of gold nanoparticles exhibiting anticancer activity against breast cancer cells [40]. Despite these promising advances primarily focusing on wound dressings, antibacterial materials, ionic conductors, and tissue regeneration the potential of JF-based biopolymers as enzyme immobilization platforms, particularly in electrospun nanofiber systems, remains insufficiently explored.

While these studies highlight the multifunctionality of JF-based materials, most of them have focused on biomedical, electronic, or separation applications. In contrast, the use of JF-derived biopolymers as enzyme immobilization platforms particularly in electrospun nanofiber systems has not been adequately explored. Furthermore, although other sources of collagen-like proteins such as algae are also available, Rhopilema nomadica offers a unique opportunity due to its abundance as an invasive Lessepsian species. This jellyfish entered the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal in the 1970s and established populations in the SE Levantine Basin [41]. It was first recorded in 1995 off the Mersin coast of Türkiye [42] and subsequently in İskenderun Bay [43]. Since then, large concentrations of JF have been observed on the Mediterranean coast of Türkiye, especially during the summer months [44]. In this study, nanofibers composed of PVA and varying ratios of JF (Rhopilema nomadica) derived biopolymer were fabricated via electrospinning (Fig. 1 ). The composite nanofibers were characterized using FTIR, SEM, TGA, and DSC techniques. Laccase was immobilized onto selected nanofiber supports, and their performance in the enzymatic removal of BPA was evaluated. The rationale for selecting jellyfish as the raw material lies not only in its favorable physicochemical properties (such as hydrophilicity and gel-forming ability), but also in the urgent need to valorize an ecologically harmful invasive species. This study thus aims to offer a novel, sustainable solution that integrates material innovation with environmental responsibility.

Polyvinyl alcohol (PVA, Mw ≈ 130,000, 99 % hydrolyzed), laccase (≥0.5 U/mg) from Trametes versicolor, 2,2′-azino-bis(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid) (ABTS), glutaraldehyde solution (GA, 25 % in H2O), bisphenol A (BPA, 2,2-Bis(4-hydroxyphenyl)propane, ≥99 %), Triton X-100, bovine serum albumin (BSA), sodium acetate (CH3COONa), monobasic potassium phosphate (KH2PO4), dibasic potassium phosphate (K2HPO4), and sodium citrate (Na3C6H5O7) were all purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (USA). All other chemicals and reagents used were of analytical grade and the highest available purity. Deionized water was used throughout the preparation of all aqueous solutions.

Rhopilema nomadica samples were obtained from trawl and purse seine fishermen in Mersin Bay and brought to Muğla Sıtkı Koçman University, Faculty of Fisheries, Marine Biology Laboratory via cold chain. Mouth arms and tentacles were removed and umbrella parts of all samples were stored in deep freezers at −18 °C. JF tissues thawed at 4 °C before use and cleaned thoroughly under running water. Then the tissues were mixed in a homogenizer for 15 min. The sample was centrifuged at 4100 rpm for 30 min. The supernatant was received and transferred to the Faculty of Science, Chemistry Department at 4 °C for preparation of JF-NanoMats.

JF-Nanomats were fabricated by electrospinning blends of PVA and JF derived biopolymer at varying concentrations. A 12 % (w/v) PVA stock solution was prepared by dissolving PVA in deionized water at 90 °C under constant stirring for 3 h. Separately, JF extracts were prepared at 10 %, 50 %, and 100 % (w/w) concentrations by dispersing the dried JF material in 2 % (v/v) acetic acid solution under stirring at room temperature for 1 h. To obtain the final electrospinning solutions, the PVA and JF solutions were mixed at equal volumes, resulting in a fixed PVA concentration of 6 % (w/v) and final JF concentrations of 5 %, 25 %, and 50 % (w/w), respectively. The resulting formulations were denoted as PVA/JF5, PVA/JF25, and PVA/JF50. PVA (6 %, w/v) served as the control formulation. Electrospinning was performed using a horizontal setup equipped with a 10 mL syringe and a 22-gauge stainless steel needle. To improve fiber formation, 1 % (v/v) Triton X-100 was added to the final polymer solutions and briefly mixed prior to electrospinning. The mixtures were then transferred into syringes and processed using an electrospinning system (Inovenso Nanospinner) equipped with a syringe pump (New Era Pump Systems Inc.). Electrospinning was conducted under varying process conditions, including needle to collector distances (10–17 cm), applied voltages (12–19 kV), and flow rates (0.4–1.2 mL/h), which were optimized for each formulation to ensure uniform and bead-free fiber morphology. All electrospinning procedures were conducted at room temperature under ambient humidity. The obtained JF-NanoMats were air dried and stored in a desiccator until further use.

The chemical structure and surface functional groups of the fabricated JF-NanoMats were characterized using attenuated total reflectance-Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR) with a Thermo Scientific Nicolet iS-5 spectrometer. Prior to analysis, all samples were thermally dried at 60 °C for 48 h and subsequently stored in a desiccator for an additional 24 h to minimize the influence of surface-adsorbed moisture and ensure accurate spectral interpretation. Thermal stability and decomposition behavior of both pristine materials and JF-NanoMats were investigated through thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), performed on a Perkin Elmer TGA 4000 under a nitrogen atmosphere. The samples were heated from 50 °C to 650 °C at a constant heating rate to assess their degradation profiles. Thermal transitions, including glass transition and melting behavior, were further examined via differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) using a Perkin Elmer Jade DSC instrument. Analyses were conducted from 30 °C to 350 °C with a heating rate of 10 °C/min under an argon purge (200 mL/min). DSC thermograms were recorded and analyzed using Pyris software. The surface morphology of JF-NanoMats was examined by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (JEOL JSM 7600F), available at the Muğla Sıtkı Koçman University Advanced Technologies Application and Research Center. Average fiber diameters were determined by manually measuring 100 randomly selected fibers using ImageJ software. Diameter distribution histograms and mean values were generated using OriginPro 2019. To assess the surface area and porosity of the nanofiber mats, SEM images were analyzed using ImageJ software (NIH, USA). Prior to imaging, all samples (PVA, PVA/JF5, and PVA/JF25) were thermally dried at 60 °C for 48 h and subsequently stored in a desiccator for 24 h to minimize moisture-related artifacts. SEM micrographs were then captured at identical magnification levels (×10,000) from five randomly selected regions across each nanofiber mat to ensure representative sampling. Each image was binarized and processed using the “Analyze Particles” function in ImageJ to quantify the surface area and porosity. The final values reported for each sample represent the average ± standard deviation of five independent measurements.

JF-NanoMats are inherently water-soluble, necessitating a cross-linking step to improve their structural stability in aqueous environments. Cross-linking was achieved using GA, which reacts with hydroxyl groups present in PVA and functional groups within JF-NanoMats. A non-aqueous GA solution (1.4 %, v/v) was prepared by mixing 7 mL of 25 % GA, 0.5 mL of 37 % hydrochloric acid, and 117.5 mL of acetone. JF-NanoMats were exposed to GA vapor in a closed chamber at room temperature for 24 h. Following cross-linking, JF-NanoMats were washed thoroughly with deionized water several times to remove residual GA and unreacted reagents. The cross-linked JF-NanoMats were then dried at room temperature and stored in a desiccator prior to use.

The activity of free laccase was determined using a modified version of a previously reported spectrophotometric method, employing ABTS as the chromogenic substrate [45]. The reaction mixture consisted of 900 μL of sodium acetate buffer (50 mM, pH 5) and 100 μL of 1 mM ABTS. The reaction was initiated by the addition of 10 μL of free laccase solution and incubated at 25 °C for 10 min. The change in absorbance at 420 nm was recorded, and enzyme activity was calculated using the molar extinction coefficient of ABTS (ε = 36,000 M−1 cm−1). One unit of laccase activity (U) was defined as the amount of enzyme required to oxidize 1 μmol of ABTS per min under the specified conditions. The activity of immobilized laccase was measured using 10 mg of enzyme loaded JF-NanoMats, mixed with 800 μL of sodium acetate buffer (50 mM, pH 5) and 100 μL of 1 mM ABTS solution. The reaction mixture was incubated at 25 °C for 10 min. After incubation, the immobilized enzyme was separated by centrifugation at 10,000 rpm for 2 min, and the absorbance of the supernatant was measured at 420 nm. Laccase was immobilized onto JF-NanoMats through a two-step process consisting of adsorption followed by GA mediated cross-linking. To evaluate the suitability of different nanofiber formulations, 15 mg of each nanofiber type (PVA, PVA/JF5, and PVA/JF25) was incubated with 1 mL of laccase solution at various concentrations (0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 mg/mL). ce:section.ce:section-title: Characterization of immobilized laccase on JF-NanoMats
ce:section.ce:para: The catalytic performance of free and immobilized laccase was systematically characterized to assess the effects of immobilization on its biochemical properties. The optimal temperature for both free and immobilized laccase was determined by measuring enzymatic activity at various temperatures ranging from 20 °C to 75 °C using ABTS as the substrate in 50 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH 5.0).

To evaluate thermal stability, enzyme samples were incubated at 50 °C, and 60 °C. Residual activity was measured at 30 min intervals to monitor time-dependent changes in enzyme functionality. Comparisons were made between free laccase and laccase immobilized on JF-NanoMats.

The enzymatic activity of free and immobilized laccase was assessed over a pH range of 3.0–9.0 using 50 mM buffers (sodium citrate, sodium acetate, phosphate, and Tris-HCl) to determine the optimal pH. Enzyme activity was assayed after incubation at 25 °C to identify the pH at which catalytic performance peaked. To assess pH stability, free and immobilized laccase samples were pre-incubated at different pH values for 1 h, after which their residual activities were determined under standard assay conditions.

The reusability of immobilized laccase was investigated over 12 consecutive catalytic cycles. After each cycle, the nanofiber mats were washed with 50 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH 5.0) to remove residual substrate, and the retained activity was measured in the following cycle to evaluate operational stability and reusability.

The storage stability of both free and immobilized laccase was assessed over a 30-day period under two different storage temperatures (4 °C and 25 °C). Enzyme samples were periodically removed, and their residual activities were measured using standard assay conditions to evaluate long-term storage stability.

The kinetic parameters, including the Michaelis-Menten constant (K m) and the maximum reaction rate (V max), were determined by measuring enzymatic activity in the presence of ABTS at various concentrations (0.1–1 mM). The data were fitted to a Lineweaver-Burk plot to calculate K m and V max values for both free and immobilized laccase.

Laccase was immobilized onto three nanofiber mat compositions (PVA, PVA/JF5, and PVA/JF25) using a standardized immobilization protocol for all systems in order to ensure comparability. Specifically, 15 mg of nanofiber was incubated with 1 mg/mL laccase solution for 120 min to allow for adsorption, followed by 120 min of crosslinking with 4 % (v/v) GA. Although previous optimization studies had revealed slight differences in the immobilization efficiency of each nanofiber formulation, in this study we employed identical immobilization parameters across all samples to eliminate variability introduced by protocol differences. This approach was adopted to support a scientifically valid comparison of catalytic performance. All BPA degradation experiments were conducted under unified reaction conditions (pH 4.5 and 35 °C), which correspond to the optimal catalytic activity of the free laccase. This approach was adopted to enable accurate benchmarking of catalytic efficiency, substrate tolerance, and operational stability between the free and immobilized enzyme systems.

The reactions were carried out in 250 mL Erlenmeyer flasks containing 100 mL of 50 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH 4.5) and 20 mg L−1 BPA. The mixtures were incubated in an orbital shaker at 125 rpm in the absence of light to prevent photodegradation. Aliquots (1 mL) were withdrawn at predetermined intervals (15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, 120, and 150 min), and the remaining BPA concentration was quantified colorimetrically using a method based on the reaction with 4-aminoantipyrine and potassium ferricyanide at pH 7.9. The resulting quinone-type complex was measured at 507 nm using a UV–Vis spectrophotometer [47].

To evaluate the effect of substrate load, BPA degradation assays were also conducted at initial concentrations of 5, 10, 20, and 40 mg L−1, under the same standardized reaction conditions. Operational stability was assessed by reusing the immobilized systems over 10 consecutive degradation cycles. After each cycle, the nanofiber mats were rinsed thoroughly with buffer and reused under identical conditions (20 mg L−1 BPA, pH 4.5, 35 °C, 120 min). The BPA removal efficiency after each cycle was recorded to evaluate the retained catalytic activity and reusability of each immobilized system.

This strictly standardized methodology ensured that observed differences in catalytic performance and stability could be attributed solely to the nature of the immobilization matrix, rather than to external reaction variables. As such, the study provides a reliable comparative evaluation of the three nanofiber-supported laccase systems against the free enzyme.

All experiments were performed in triplicate (n = 3), and the results are expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Error bars in the relevant figures represent the standard deviation from the mean values. Statistical reproducibility was ensured by repeating each assay independently under identical conditions.

The efficiency of enzyme immobilization is significantly influenced by the structural and physicochemical properties of the support material [48]. Among various immobilization carriers, electrospun nanofibers have attracted considerable attention due to their high surface-to-volume ratio, tunable porosity, and customizable morphology, offering an ideal platform for biocatalytic applications [49]. In this study, nanofibers were fabricated using PVA as the base polymer and JF-based biopolymer at different incorporation ratios (5 %, 25 %, and 50 %, w/w), yielding PVA, PVA/JF5, PVA/JF25, and PVA/JF50 formulations, respectively. The electrospinning process was optimized for each composition to ensure the formation of uniform, bead-free nanofibers with adequate mechanical integrity. Key process parameters including flow rate, applied voltage, and needle-to-collector distance were systematically adjusted based on the solution behavior and electrospinning stability [50,51]. As shown in Table 1 , increasing JF content required a gradual increase in all process parameters, likely due to increased solution viscosity and altered conductivity. For example, while pure PVA was electrospun at 0.4 mL/h and 12 kV, the PVA/JF50 solution required higher values of 1.2 mL/h and 19 kV to achieve a stable Taylor cone and continuous fiber formation. The electrospinning parameters demonstrated a clear trend with increasing JF content, which required gradual adjustments in flow rate, applied voltage, and working distance. This can be attributed primarily to the changes in the rheological and physicochemical properties of the spinning solutions. Specifically, the incorporation of JF increased the viscosity and possibly altered the conductivity of the mixtures, both of which are known to significantly influence the electrospinning behavior. This increase in conductivity may be attributed to the presence of ionizable groups (e.g., carboxyl, amino) in the jellyfish-derived proteins, which contribute to the overall ionic strength of the spinning solution and enhance its charge-carrying capacity during electrospinning. Higher viscosity generally requires an increased flow rate to ensure adequate jet formation, while increased conductivity demands higher voltage to sustain the Taylor cone and initiate fiber elongation. Additionally, the need for longer tip-to-collector distances in JF rich formulations (e.g., 17 cm for PVA/JF50 vs. 10 cm for pure PVA) reflects the increased flight time required for solvent evaporation in more viscous solutions. Despite these parameter optimizations, the PVA/JF50 system failed to produce uniform nanofibers, most likely due to excessive solution viscosity or instability in jet formation under high-voltage conditions, resulting in bead formation and disrupted fiber morphology. This supports the critical role of solution formulation in achieving electrospinning success and further highlights the practical limitation of overly high JF loading.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Chemical, thermal, and morphological characterization of JF-NanoMats
ce:section.ce:para: FTIR spectroscopy was employed to investigate the functional groups present in the nanofiber composites and to explore the molecular interactions between PVA and JF-derived biopolymer across different blend ratios. In order to reduce the influence of moisture and eliminate potential artifacts related to surface-adsorbed water, all samples were subjected to thermal drying at 60 °C for 48 h and stored in a desiccator for an additional 24 h prior to analysis. The resulting spectra for pure PVA, JF, and JF-NanoMats (PVA/JF5, PVA/JF25, and PVA/JF50) are presented in Fig. 2 .

The spectrum of neat PVA exhibited well-defined characteristic bands at 3280 cm−1 (OH stretching), 2912 cm−1 (CH stretching), and 1100–1435 cm−1 (CO and CH bending vibrations), in agreement with previous reports on PVA-based polymers [52,53]. The FTIR spectrum of the JF biopolymer displayed a broad band centered around 3305 cm−1, corresponding to overlapping OH and NH stretching modes, which are indicative of hydroxyl and amide groups commonly found in protein-rich gelatinous matrices [54]. A strong absorption at 1622 cm−1, attributed to amide I (CO stretching), reflects the presence of polypeptide backbones, while the band near 1095 cm−1 corresponds to CO stretching in polysaccharide or glycoprotein components [55]. In the composite nanofibers, the FTIR spectra reveal a combination of vibrational features originating from both PVA and JF, with notable shifts and intensity variations indicating the occurrence of intermolecular interactions. Specifically, the O-H/N-H stretching band progressively shifts in position across the hybrid compositions: 3315 cm−1 (PVA/JF5), 3375 cm−1 (PVA/JF25), and 3350 cm−1 (PVA/JF50). These shifts, observed in dried samples with minimal moisture interference, suggest an increasing degree of hydrogen bonding or dipolar interactions between hydroxyl groups in PVA and amide, carboxyl, or other polar groups in JF. Furthermore, the amide I band becomes more prominent and shifts slightly from 1675 cm−1 (PVA/JF5) to cm−1 (PVA/JF50), indicating increased protein content and stronger backbone-related vibrations in higher JF compositions. The CN and NH deformation bands observed in the region 1100–1150 cm cm−1 (e.g., 1101–1110 cm−1) also intensify with increasing JF content, supporting the incorporation of amino acid-based functional groups into the nanofiber matrix. Additionally, no significant absorption was observed in the 2000–2200 cm−1 region, suggesting the absence of overtone or combination bands typically associated with moisture or protein-related structural irregularities [56,57]. Collectively, these spectral changes confirm successful chemical blending between PVA and JF and reveal a composition-dependent evolution of the molecular environment within the electrospun nanofibers. The results provide evidence for hybrid biopolymer network formation driven by non-covalent interactions such as hydrogen bonding and polar group association.

TGA and dTGA were performed to evaluate the thermal stability and decomposition behavior of pure PVA, JF, and JF-NanoMats. The results are presented in Fig. 3 . The TGA curve of pure PVA exhibited a typical three-step weight loss profile. The first stage, observed around 125 °C, is associated with the evaporation of adsorbed moisture [58]. The second, and most significant, degradation stage begins at approximately 290 °C and corresponds to the elimination reactions and depolymerization of the PVA backbone [59]. A third, smaller degradation event occurs near 440 °C, which is attributed to the breakdown of carbonaceous residues and possibly residual crosslinked structures [60]. In contrast, the JF sample displayed a slower and more continuous thermal degradation profile, with a major decomposition peak centered at 325 °C, characteristic of proteinaceous biomaterials such as gelatin or collagen. The broad transition suggests a heterogeneous composition and gradual breakdown of polypeptide chains [61,62]. The JF-NanoMats exhibited complex, multi-step degradation patterns reflecting the contributions of both PVA and JF components. Initial mass losses in the 82–90 °C range were observed in all composites and are associated with moisture and volatile components. Subsequent thermal events appeared in two main regions: around 230–265 °C, related to the partial degradation of JF-derived peptides, and 375–451 °C, corresponding to sequential decomposition of PVA and remaining biopolymer fractions. Among the composites, PVA/JF25 demonstrated the most thermally stable profile, with sharp and well-defined degradation peaks at 352 °C and 415 °C, and a delayed onset of final decomposition. This improved thermal stability can be attributed to stronger intermolecular interactions, such as hydrogen bonding between PVA and JF, which likely enhanced structural integrity a finding that is consistent with FTIR results. Overall, the incorporation of JF substantially modified the thermal degradation behavior of PVA nanofibers. The composite containing 25 % JF (w/w) offered the optimal balance between biopolymer integration and thermal resistance, highlighting its potential suitability as a support matrix for enzyme immobilization or other thermally demanding biotechnological applications.

DSC was employed to investigate the thermal transitions, crystallinity, and the influence of JF biopolymer incorporation on the thermal behavior of PVA nanofiber and JF-NanoMats. Fig. 4 shows the DSC thermograms, revealing distinct thermal events associated with moisture loss, glass transition (Tg), melting (Tm), and degradation-related transitions. The DSC thermogram of pure PVA displayed a broad endothermic peak around 225 °C, which corresponds to the melting of crystalline PVA regions, and a secondary transition near 325 °C related to thermal degradation [63,64]. The JF-based biopolymer sample showed characteristic thermal events at lower temperatures (147–175 °C), typically associated with protein denaturation and water loss [65]. Upon incorporation of JF into the PVA matrix, notable shifts in thermal transitions were observed. PVA/JF5 nanofiber exhibited multiple transitions, including moisture loss at 75 °C, a melting transition near 220 °C, and degradation-related events at 275 °C. As JF content increased, the glass transition temperature (Tg) gradually shifted upward (from 100 °C in PVA/JF25 to 110 °C in PVA/JF50), suggesting reduced polymer chain mobility due to increased intermolecular interactions, likely hydrogen bonding between PVA and JF components. The melting transitions (Tm) also broadened and slightly shifted with higher JF content, indicating a disruption of PVA's crystalline regions and the formation of a more amorphous composite structure. This decrease in crystallinity is consistent with the FTIR and TGA results and further supports the successful incorporation and interaction of JF within the nanofiber network.

Fig. 5 presents SEM micrographs of electrospun nanofibers fabricated with increasing concentrations of JF extract. The PVA nanofiber (Fig. 5a) exhibit a smooth, bead-free morphology with uniform fiber diameters, indicating optimal electrospinning conditions and stable jet formation. Upon incorporation of PVA/JF5 (Fig. 5b), the fiber structure remains largely homogeneous, though a slight increase in fiber thickness is observed, suggesting minimal disruption in spinning behavior. For PVA/JF25 (Fig. 5c), the fibers become noticeably thinner, yet maintain a continuous, interconnected network with occasional junctions likely reflecting increased solution conductivity and slight molecular incompatibility. In contrast, PVA/JF50 (Fig. 5d) display significant morphological deterioration, including bead formation, irregular fiber diameters, and an overall loss of structural uniformity. These defects are indicative of electrospinning instability due to excessive alterations in solution rheology and phase separation at high JF loading. Consequently, PVA/JF50 fibers were excluded from further functionalization studies, such as enzyme immobilization, due to their compromised structural integrity.

Fiber diameter distribution graphs derived from SEM measurements for each formulation are provided in the Supplementary Material as Fig. S1 (PVA), Fig. S2 (PVA/JF5), and Fig. S3 (PVA/JF25), confirming a consistent reduction in average diameter with increasing JF content. As the JF content increased from 0 % to 25 %, a progressive decrease in fiber diameter was observed from 558.75 nm for pure PVA to 376.92 nm and 331.01 nm for PVA/JF5 and PVA/JF25, respectively. This reduction is associated with enhanced solution conductivity and stretching during electrospinning, resulting in finer fibers.

The surface morphology and porosity of the nanofiber mats were further analyzed using ImageJ software based on SEM micrographs. As summarized in Table 2 , both surface area and porosity increased significantly with the incorporation of JF. PVA nanofibers exhibited a surface area of 172.99 ± 13.26 μm2 and porosity of 12.52 ± 1.22 %. With the addition of 5 % JF (PVA/JF5), these values increased to 190.30 ± 16.48 μm2 and 15.45 ± 1.87 %, respectively. The highest values were observed in the PVA/JF25 sample, with a surface area of 270.84 ± 20.42 μm2 and porosity of 32.08 ± 2.18 %. As the JF content increased from 0 % to 25 %, a significant enhancement in both surface area and porosity was observed, as summarized in Table 2. The surface area rose from 172.99 ± 13.26 μm2 for pure PVA to 270.84 ± 20.42 μm2 for PVA/JF₂₅, while porosity values increased from 12.52 ± 1.22 % to 32.08 ± 2.18 %. These enhancements in surface characteristics suggest that the incorporation of JF promotes the formation of a more open and porous fiber network, which may facilitate improved substrate accessibility and enzyme-substrate interactions factors that are critical for catalytic applications such as BPA degradation.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Systematic optimization studies of laccase immobilized JF-NanoMats
ce:section.ce:para: The influence of laccase concentration on immobilization efficiency was investigated using five different enzyme loadings (0.25, 0.50, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 mg/mL), while maintaining all other experimental parameters constant: 10 mg of nanofiber mat, 30 min of adsorption time, 30 min of crosslinking time, and 3 % (v/v) GA as the crosslinking agent. As presented in Fig. 6 , the specific activity of all nanofiber types increased with rising enzyme concentrations up to a critical threshold, beyond which further increases led to a decline in activity. For PVA nanofiber, the highest specific activity (14.87 U/g) was recorded at 1.0 mg/mL; further increases in laccase concentration resulted in a gradual decline, most likely due to diffusion limitations or enzyme crowding on the fiber surface. This result could be explained by the previous observation that a high free laccase concentration can enhance the intermolecular steric hindrance, which restrains the diffusion of substrates and products [66]. In comparison, PVA/JF5 nanofiber exhibited their maximum activity (26.42 U/g) also at 1.0 mg/mL, whereas PVA/JF25 nanofiber displayed the highest overall performance, with a peak specific activity of 34.59 U/g at 2.0 mg/mL. These results demonstrate that both the enzyme loading and nanofiber composition play critical roles in determining immobilization efficiency, and that PVA/JF25 nanofiber represent a particularly effective platform for high-capacity, high-activity enzyme immobilization.

Similar trends regarding the effect of enzyme concentration on immobilization performance have been reported in previous studies. In a study involving the immobilization of laccase onto activated carbon fibers (ACFs) and dopamine-functionalized activated carbon fibers (DA-ACFs), enzyme concentrations ranging from 0.5 to 5 g/L were tested. The results indicated that specific activity increased with enzyme concentration up to 2 g/L, after which a gradual decline was observed, attributed to steric hindrance and limited substrate diffusion at high enzyme loadings [67]. Likewise, another study using enzyme concentrations between 0.5 and 4 mg/mL immobilized laccase onto functionalized cellulose nanofiber–calcium alginate (FCNF-CA) beads. It was found that enzyme activity reached its maximum at 2 mg/mL, while further increases in enzyme concentration led to reduced activity [68]. These findings are in strong agreement with the present study and further support the notion that excessive enzyme loading can hinder catalytic efficiency due to diffusion limitations and enzyme crowding on the support surface.

To determine the optimal amount of nanofiber material for laccase immobilization, varying fiber masses (10, 12.5, 15, 17.5, and 20 mg) were tested while keeping all other parameters constant, including enzyme concentration (2.0 mg/mL), adsorption time (30 min), crosslinking time (30 min), and GA concentration (3 %). As illustrated in Fig. 7a, the specific activity increased with the amount of nanofiber up to a certain point, after which a decline was observed. For PVA/JF25 nanofiber, the maximum specific activity (38.45 U/g) was obtained at 12.5 mg, followed by a gradual decrease, likely due to an excess of surface area leading to suboptimal enzyme distribution or diffusion limitations. A similar pattern was observed for PVA/JF5 nanofiber, where the highest activity (32.66 U/g) was recorded at 15 mg. In contrast, PVA nanofiber exhibited their peak activity (26.48 U/g) at 17.5 mg. These differences highlight the role of dopamine incorporation in improving immobilization efficiency, enabling higher enzymatic activity to be achieved with lower support mass. However, further increases in nanofiber quantity may lead to enzyme dilution across the surface, steric hindrance, or restricted substrate accessibility, all of which can reduce the effective catalytic interaction.

Similar observations have been reported in the literature regarding the effect of support material quantity on enzyme immobilization performance. In a study involving laccase immobilization onto sodium alginate beads, the optimal carrier amount was found to be 200 mg, beyond which no further improvement in enzymatic activity was observed [69]. Likewise, several studies on nanofiber-based immobilization platforms have shown that increasing the amount of support material initially enhances enzyme activity due to greater surface area and higher enzyme loading capacity. However, beyond a critical threshold, further increases in support mass often lead to a decline in activity. This phenomenon is commonly attributed to reduced enzyme density on the surface, which can weaken enzyme substrate interactions, as well as to diffusional limitations and steric hindrance caused by excessive surface area and poor enzyme distribution [49,70,71].

The effect of adsorption time on the activity of immobilized laccase was investigated over a range of contact durations (30 to 180 min), while keeping all other experimental parameters constant, including enzyme concentration (2.0 mg/mL), nanofiber amount (10 mg), crosslinking time (30 min), and GA concentration (3 %). As illustrated in Fig. 7b, the specific activity of immobilized laccase increased with adsorption time up to an optimal point, after which a gradual decline was observed. For PVA nanofiber, the maximum specific activity (48.99 U/g) was obtained at 150 min. In contrast, PVA/JF5 and PVA/JF25 nanofibers exhibited their peak activities earlier, at 120 min, with specific activity values of 53.09 U/g and 59.69 U/g, respectively. The initial rise in activity with prolonged contact time is likely due to enhanced enzyme surface interactions and improved adsorption kinetics, allowing greater enzyme uptake. However, beyond the optimal duration, potential enzyme desorption, conformational instability, or surface saturation may reduce effective catalytic activity. Notably, PVA/JF25 nanofiber consistently outperformed the other support types at all time points, emphasizing their superior surface morphology and higher affinity for enzyme immobilization. Based on these findings, an adsorption time of 120 min was determined to be optimal for subsequent immobilization experiments.

Similar findings regarding the effect of adsorption time on immobilized laccase activity have been reported in previous studies. For instance, in a study involving the immobilization of laccase onto multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs), a short adsorption duration of 30 min was found to be sufficient for achieving maximum enzyme activity [72]. In contrast, laccase immobilized onto polyamide 6 nanofibers through combined adsorption and crosslinking methods showed optimal activity at 3 h of contact time [73]. Likewise, in a separate study employing modified cellulose/cellulose fibril beads as the immobilization support, maximum laccase activity was observed after an adsorption time of 3 h [26]. These differences can be attributed to variations in support material properties such as porosity, surface chemistry, and enzyme affinity. Overall, these findings support the present results, in which an optimal adsorption time of 120 min was identified for PVA/JF25 nanofibers. Extended contact beyond this point may lead to enzyme desorption, conformational instability, or surface saturation, ultimately reducing catalytic performance.

To evaluate the impact of crosslinking duration on the catalytic performance of immobilized laccase, a series of experiments were carried out using various reaction times ranging from 30 to 180 min, with 3 % GA serving as the crosslinking agent. All other experimental parameters including enzyme concentration (2.0 mg/mL), nanofiber mass (10 mg), and adsorption time (120 min) were kept constant. As shown in Fig. 7c, the specific activity of immobilized laccase was markedly influenced by the duration of the crosslinking step. For PVA nanofiber, enzymatic activity gradually increased with time, reaching a maximum of 52.98 U/g at 150 min, followed by a slight decline at 180 min. PVA/JF5 nanofiber exhibited a similar pattern but attained their peak activity (56.62 U/g) earlier, at 90 min. In contrast, PVA/JF25 nanofiber demonstrated superior performance, achieving the highest specific activity (64.89 U/g) at just 60 min. Beyond this point, activity progressively declined, which is likely due to over-crosslinking effects such as steric hindrance, enzyme structural rigidity, or partial inactivation. These results indicate that although crosslinking is essential to stabilize the enzyme structure and enhance immobilization efficiency, excessively long crosslinking durations can impair catalytic function by limiting the enzyme's conformational flexibility.

The effect of crosslinking time on immobilization efficiency has been explored in various laccase immobilization studies. In a study using chitosan beads as the support for Trametes pubescens laccase, the optimal crosslinking duration was reported to be 3 h, after which no significant improvement in enzymatic activity was observed [74]. In contrast, a study involving the immobilization of bacterial laccase onto magnetic dialdehyde cellulose particles found that enzyme activity continued to increase up to 12 h of crosslinking time, indicating a slower reaction between the enzyme and the support matrix [75]. These discrepancies highlight the importance of the immobilization matrix and its functional chemistry in determining the optimal crosslinking duration. The current study similarly demonstrated that excessive crosslinking can lead to a decline in enzymatic activity, likely due to steric hindrance, enzyme rigidity, or partial inactivation.

GA is widely employed as a bifunctional crosslinking agent for enzyme immobilization due to its ability to form covalent bonds between enzyme molecules and support surfaces, thereby enhancing enzyme stability. In this study, the effect of varying GA concentrations (1–5 %, v/v) on laccase activity was investigated using three different electrospun nanofiber supports: PVA, PVA/JF5, and PVA/JF25. As shown in Fig. 7d, all supports exhibited a similar trend specific activity increased with GA concentration up to an optimal point, beyond which a notable decrease in activity was observed. The initial enhancement in enzymatic activity is attributed to improved immobilization efficiency resulting from more effective covalent bonding between the enzyme and the support surface. At low GA concentrations, insufficient crosslinking may result in weak enzyme attachment, enzyme leaching, or suboptimal enzyme orientation. As the GA concentration increases, a denser and more stable enzyme support network is formed, improving structural rigidity and catalytic performance. However, at concentrations exceeding the optimum, a decrease in activity was recorded. This decline is most likely due to over-crosslinking, which may induce conformational constraints near the active site, steric hindrance, or even partial denaturation of the protein structure. Excessive crosslinking can also reduce the molecular flexibility of the enzyme, which is essential for substrate binding and turnover, particularly in the case of multi‑copper oxidases such as laccase. Interestingly, the optimal GA concentration varied among the different nanofiber types. For PVA/JF25 nanofiber, the highest specific activity (69.91 U/g) was achieved at 3 % GA, whereas PVA and PVA/JF5 exhibited their maximum activities (56.96 U/g and 62.83 U/g, respectively) at 4 %. This variation can be attributed to the distinct physicochemical characteristics of each support. PVA/JF25 nanofiber, with their higher surface area and porosity (as demonstrated in Table 1), likely provided better enzyme accessibility and stronger enzyme support interactions, enabling effective immobilization even at lower GA concentrations. In contrast, the relatively denser structure of PVA and the lower porosity of PVA/JF5 may have required higher crosslinker concentrations to attain comparable immobilization efficiency. These results suggest that the optimal GA concentration is strongly support dependent and closely related to the structural and morphological features of the nanofiber matrix.

Comparable findings have been reported in previous studies investigating the influence of glutaraldehyde concentration on laccase immobilization. In a study where laccase derived from Trametes versicolor was chemically crosslinked onto chitosan beads, the optimal GA concentration was determined to be 2 % (v/v). Beyond this point, no further improvement in enzymatic activity was observed [76]. Similarly, another study exploring GA concentrations ranging from 0.1 % to 1.0 % (v/v) reported that enzyme activity increased gradually with GA concentration, reaching a peak at 0.8 %, after which it declined. The observed decrease was attributed to excessive crosslinking reactions at higher GA concentrations, which are known to induce conformational changes in enzyme molecules. These alterations can disrupt the active site architecture, reduce structural flexibility, and ultimately impair catalytic efficiency [74]. These findings are in agreement with the current study, in which an optimal GA concentration of 3 % was observed for PVA/JF25 nanofiber, highlighting the importance of fine-tuning crosslinker concentration to preserve enzymatic functionality while ensuring stable immobilization.

The immobilization performance of laccase on different electrospun nanofiber supports PVA, PVA/JF5, and PVA/JF25 was evaluated under their respective optimized conditions, and the results are summarized in Table 3 . Among the tested supports, PVA/JF25 exhibited the highest specific activity (69.91 ± 1.08 U/g), followed by PVA/JF5 (62.83 ± 1.59 U/g) and PVA (56.96 ± 1.22 U/g). A similar trend was observed in terms of protein loading and enzyme immobilization capacity: PVA/JF25 achieved the greatest bound protein amount (0.942 ± 0.037 mg) and immobilization capacity (8.63 ± 0.048 mg/mg nanofiber). Notably, the immobilization yield also increased proportionally with the JF-based biopolymer content, reaching 56.42 ± 1.34 % for PVA/JF25, in contrast to only 32.48 ± 1.12 % for unmodified PVA (Table 3). These findings emphasize the critical role of nanofiber composition and surface morphology in influencing immobilization efficiency. Importantly, PVA/JF25 achieved its highest performance using lower nanofiber mass (12.5 mg) and a milder crosslinking condition (3 % GA), while still outperforming other formulations. In contrast, the PVA nanofiber support required comparatively harsher immobilization conditions including higher enzyme concentrations, longer adsorption and crosslinking durations, and an increased GA concentration to achieve lower specific activity values. This indicates that the incorporation of JF-based biopolymers significantly enhances the functional properties of electrospun nanofibers, enabling more efficient and less chemically intensive immobilization strategies.

Following the optimization of immobilization parameters, comprehensive characterization studies were conducted to evaluate the functional and operational properties of the immobilized laccase systems. These analyses are essential for elucidating the effects of immobilization on enzymatic behavior under varying environmental conditions and for determining the practical feasibility of the developed biocatalysts in applications. Characterization involved assessing several critical parameters, including optimum pH and temperature, pH and thermal stability, operational reusability, storage stability, and kinetic constants. These evaluations provide insight into the structural integrity and catalytic resilience of immobilized enzymes relative to their free counterparts. Furthermore, the comparative performance of different nanofiber supports PVA, PVA/JF5, and PVA/JF25 was systematically analyzed under identical conditions, allowing for the identification of the most effective support matrix for potential industrial and environmental applications.

The influence of temperature on the catalytic activity of free and immobilized laccase was investigated across a temperature range of 20–75 °C to determine both the optimal operating temperature and the thermal tolerance of the enzyme systems. As illustrated in Fig. 8a, all samples exhibited increased activity with rising temperature up to a specific optimum, followed by a gradual decline at higher temperatures. The free enzyme reached its maximum activity at 35 °C. In contrast, all immobilized variants showed a modest shift in optimum temperature toward higher values, indicating enhanced thermal resistance as a result of immobilization. Among the immobilized systems, laccase immobilized PVA/JF25 nanofiber demonstrated the highest thermal performance, exhibiting 100 % relative activity at 45 °C and retaining over 76 % of its initial activity even at 60 °C. In comparison, PVA and PVA/JF5 displayed their peak activities at 40 °C but experienced more rapid activity losses at elevated temperatures. This effect was particularly pronounced in the PVA supported enzyme, which retained only 34 % activity at 65 °C. The improved thermal stability of the PVA/JF25 system is likely attributable to the physicochemical characteristics of the support, including its increased surface area and porosity. These properties may contribute to more effective enzyme encapsulation, reduced conformational mobility, and enhanced resistance to thermal denaturation. Collectively, these results suggest that enzyme immobilization particularly using JF-based nanofibers can substantially extend the functional temperature range of laccase, enhancing its suitability for applications operating under elevated thermal conditions.

Similar observations regarding the influence of immobilization on the thermal behavior of laccase have been reported in previous studies. In one study, laccase was immobilized onto magnetic cellulose composite microspheres (MC@Fe3O4), and the optimum temperature for both free and immobilized enzymes was found to be 50 °C. However, across the entire tested temperature range (20–70 °C), the immobilized enzyme consistently exhibited higher relative activity than the free enzyme, indicating improved thermal resilience due to immobilization [77]. In another study involving nanocellulose-functionalized magnetic nanoparticles as the support material, the optimum temperature shifted significantly from 35 °C for the free enzyme to 50 °C for the immobilized form [78]. This shift was attributed to enhanced structural rigidity and improved protection of the enzyme's active conformation provided by the support matrix.

The effect of pH on laccase activity was examined over a range of pH 3.0 to 9.0 using three buffer systems: acetate buffer (pH 3.0–5.5), phosphate buffer (pH 6.0–7.5), and Tris-HCl buffer (pH 8.0–9.0). As shown in Fig. 8b, the free laccase exhibited its maximum catalytic activity at pH 4.5. Upon immobilization, a slight shift or broadening in the optimal pH range was observed, depending on the nature of the support material. Laccase immobilized PVA and PVA/JF5 nanofibers retained their optimal activity at pH 4.5, similar to the free enzyme, but exhibited enhanced relative activity at both acidic and near-neutral pH values. Notably, the laccase immobilized PVA/JF25 displayed the broadest pH activity profile, achieving peak activity at pH 5.0 and maintaining over 70 % of its initial activity between pH 3.5 and 7.0. This expanded operational pH range is likely due to the protective microenvironment created by the JF-based nanofiber matrix, which may buffer the enzyme against external pH fluctuations and limit conformational destabilization. These results clearly demonstrate that enzyme immobilization, particularly on PVA/JF25 support, improves the pH tolerance and operational flexibility of laccase. Such enhancements are especially valuable in applications where pH conditions are variable or difficult to control, including wastewater treatment and industrial effluent remediation processes. These shifts in optimal pH are generally attributed to the changes in the enzyme's microenvironment upon immobilization, particularly the surface charge, hydrophilicity, and ionic interactions provided by the support material. Such modifications may alter the local proton concentration around the enzyme or affect the ionization state of residues in or near the active site, thus modifying the apparent pH optimum. Overall, these results confirm that immobilization can enhance pH stability and shift optimal catalytic conditions, thereby improving enzyme functionality in diverse or fluctuating pH environments.

Similar to the present findings, several studies have reported shifts in the optimal pH and broadened pH tolerance following laccase immobilization. In a study involving Aureobasidium pullulans laccase immobilized via the cross-linked enzyme aggregate (CLEA) method, the optimum pH shifted from 3.0 (free form) to 5.0 (immobilized form), suggesting significant stabilization in slightly less acidic conditions [79]. In another report, an enzymatic cocktail containing laccases derived from a local fungal isolate was immobilized onto a PVA/sodium alginate/lentinan (PVA/SA/LE) nanofiber matrix. The free enzyme displayed maximal activity at pH 2.0, whereas the immobilized counterpart exhibited a shifted optimum at pH 3.0 [80]. Similarly, in a study using Trametes versicolor laccase immobilized on MgFe-layered double hydroxide (LDH)/alginate composite beads, the optimum pH increased from 3.0 (free form) to 4.5 (immobilized form) [81].

The thermal stability of free and immobilized laccase was assessed by measuring residual enzymatic activity following incubation at 50 °C for up to 240 min. As shown in Fig. 8c, all enzyme systems exhibited a gradual decline in activity with increasing incubation time. However, immobilized enzymes demonstrated markedly improved thermal stability compared to the free form. After 240 min, free laccase retained only 26 % of its initial activity, whereas laccase immobilized on PVA, PVA/JF5, and PVA/JF25 nanofibers retained 31 %, 39 %, and 46 % of their initial activity, respectively. Among the immobilized systems, the PVA/JF25 supported laccase displayed the highest thermal resistance, maintaining over 68 % of its initial activity after 150 min of incubation. To further evaluate the robustness of the enzyme systems under more stringent thermal stress, residual activity was monitored at 60 °C over a period of 180 min (Fig. 8d). As expected, all enzyme forms exhibited faster activity loss at this elevated temperature. Nonetheless, immobilized enzymes particularly those on JF-based nanofibers retained significantly higher activity compared to the free enzyme. After 180 min at 60 °C, the residual activity of the free enzyme was reduced to 26 %, while immobilized laccases on PVA, PVA/JF5, and PVA/JF25 retained 35 %, 42 %, and 55 % of their original activity, respectively. The enhanced thermal stability of the PVA/JF25-based immobilized enzyme can be attributed to multiple structural and physicochemical factors. The JF derived component likely contributes to a more hydrophilic and flexible microenvironment that buffers the enzyme against thermal stress. In addition, the increased surface area and porosity of the PVA/JF25 support likely promote more stable enzyme support interactions, thereby reducing thermal denaturation and maintaining enzyme conformation. Collectively, these findings confirm that the PVA/JF25 nanofiber matrix provides an effective thermoprotective environment that extends the operational lifespan of laccase under elevated temperature conditions. These findings, while demonstrating some thermal enhancement through immobilization, also highlight that the degree of improvement strongly depends on the nature of the support matrix and the immobilization method. Compared to these systems, the PVA/JF25 nanofiber platform developed in the present study exhibited notably superior thermal stability, retaining 55 % of its activity after 180 min at 60 °C. This reinforces the importance of selecting appropriate support materials such as JF enhanced nanofibers to achieve greater enzyme stabilization under elevated temperature conditions.

Similar studies in the literature have also investigated the thermal stability of immobilized laccases under various conditions. In one study, Trametes versicolor laccase LAC was immobilized onto activated carbon derived from green coconut shell using phosphoric acid activation ACP. Thermal stability tests performed at 55 °C and 65 °C showed that after 2 h of incubation, the immobilized enzyme had lost approximately 60 % and 85 % of its initial activity, respectively [82]. In another study, Agaricus bisporus CU13 laccase immobilized on calcium alginate exhibited a 60 % loss in activity after 120 min at 50 °C, and an 80 % reduction after 90 min at 60 °C [83].

The pH stability of free and immobilized laccase was evaluated by incubating enzyme samples at various pH values (3.0–9.0) for 1 h at 25 °C, followed by measurement of residual activity under standard assay conditions. As illustrated in Fig. 8e, all enzyme forms displayed maximum stability around pH 4.5. However, the extent of activity loss at more acidic or alkaline conditions varied significantly depending on the immobilization support. The free laccase exhibited limited stability outside its optimal pH range, retaining only 26 % and 18 % of its initial activity at pH 3.0 and 9.0, respectively. In contrast, immobilized laccases demonstrated markedly enhanced stability across the entire tested pH range. Notably, laccase immobilized PVA/JF25 nanofiber retained over 50 % of its initial activity at both pH extremes. PVA/JF5 and PVA nanofibers showed reduced tolerance at pH 9.0, retaining 39 % and 29 % activity, respectively. This improved pH resilience is likely attributed to the microenvironment generated by the nanofiber support, which may buffer local pH changes and mitigate enzyme denaturation. Among all tested systems, the PVA/JF25 support exhibited the most favorable profile, maintaining a broad and relatively flat pH stability curve. This behavior is highly advantageous for biocatalytic applications where pH conditions are variable or difficult to control. Collectively, these results demonstrate that enzyme immobilization particularly on JF-based nanofiber matrices not only extends the functional pH range but also significantly improves the operational robustness of laccase under fluctuating pH environments.

The operational reusability of immobilized laccase is a key determinant of its economic feasibility and practical value in industrial biocatalysis. To evaluate this parameter, immobilized enzyme systems were subjected to consecutive catalytic cycles, and residual activity was measured following each reuse (Fig. 8f). As anticipated, all systems exhibited a progressive decline in activity with increasing cycle number; however, the extent of activity loss differed significantly depending on the support material. After 12 cycles, laccase immobilized PVA/JF25 nanofiber retained 46 % of its initial activity, while PVA/JF5 and PVA supports retained 22 % and 12 %, respectively. Notably, during the six cycles, the PVA/JF25 system preserved more than 72 % of its initial catalytic activity, demonstrating excellent operational durability. This enhanced reusability is attributed to the favorable physicochemical properties of the PVA/JF25 support specifically its porous architecture and mechanical robustness which likely reduce enzyme leaching, preserve structural integrity, and maintain strong enzyme-support interactions throughout repeated usage. These findings clearly demonstrate that JF-based nanofiber matrices, particularly PVA/JF25, significantly enhance the reusability and operational stability of immobilized laccase. This makes them promising candidates for sustainable, cost-effective applications in continuous bioprocessing and industrial wastewater treatment systems.

Comparable trends in reusability have been reported in the literature for various laccase immobilization systems. In a study where Trametes versicolor laccase was immobilized onto nanocellulose using a layer-by-layer assembly approach, the enzyme retained 55 % of its initial activity after five consecutive reuse cycles [84]. Another study involving the immobilization of laccase onto polyaniline-based nanostructures showed that after 10 cycles, the nanofiber- and nanotube-supported systems retained 61 % and 63 % of their initial activities, respectively [24]. These results reflect moderate operational durability, depending on the morphology and physicochemical nature of the support material. In a more robust system, laccase co-immobilized with zinc oxide nanoparticles on bacterial cellulose retained 80 % of its initial activity even after 10 reuse cycles [85]. This enhanced performance was attributed to synergistic stabilization provided by both the inorganic nanoparticles and the biopolymer matrix. Compared to these reports, the PVA/JF25 based immobilization system in the present study demonstrated competitive reusability, retaining 46 % activity after 12 cycles despite being subjected to more extended operational use. These findings reinforce the notion that support material composition and microstructural features play a crucial role in determining the reusability of immobilized enzymes in continuous processes.

The long-term storage stability of free and immobilized laccase was assessed at two different temperatures (4 °C and 25 °C) over a period of 30 days. Residual enzymatic activity was measured at regular intervals under standard assay conditions. As depicted in Fig. 9a and b, all enzyme forms exhibited a progressive decline in activity over time, with more pronounced degradation observed at 25 °C. However, immobilization significantly improved the storage stability of laccase compared to its free counterpart, particularly under non-refrigerated conditions. At 4 °C, the free enzyme retained only 21 % of its initial activity after 30 days, while the immobilized forms on PVA, PVA/JF5, and PVA/JF25 nanofibers retained 28 %, 32 %, and 44 % of their original activity, respectively. The stabilizing effect of immobilization was even more evident at 25 °C. Under these conditions, both the free enzyme and PVA immobilized laccase exhibited complete inactivation by day 30. In contrast, PVA/JF5 and PVA/JF25 retained 26 % and 52 % of their initial activity, respectively. These results underscore the considerable protective effect conferred by JF-based nanofiber matrices, especially PVA/JF25. The enhanced storage stability is likely due to the biocompatible and porous structure of the support, which may reduce thermal and oxidative degradation by limiting conformational flexibility and shielding the enzyme from environmental stressors. The PVA/JF25 nanofiber system thus offers a promising platform for developing storage-stable biocatalysts, particularly for applications requiring long-term shelf life without refrigeration.

Several studies have demonstrated that enzyme immobilization can markedly enhance long-term storage stability. For instance, laccase immobilized on CTAB-KOH modified biochar (CKMB) retained nearly 40 % activity after 30 days at 4 °C, whereas the free enzyme lost 80 % of its activity, highlighting the stabilizing effect of the support matrix [86]. Similarly, magnetic cellulose composite microspheres provided substantial protection, with immobilized laccase maintaining 75.31 % activity compared to 26 % in the free form after 25 days [77]. In another study using bamboo-derived biochar, the immobilized enzyme preserved 80.1 % of its initial activity after 30 days, while the free enzyme retained only 28.14 % [87]. These consistent patterns across diverse support systems clearly demonstrate that immobilization improves enzymatic shelf life by shielding the enzyme from denaturation and deactivation over time. In the present study, the PVA/JF25 nanofiber-supported laccase exhibited a similarly high level of stability, retaining substantial activity under both refrigerated and ambient conditions. This result underscores the functional advantage of using porous, biocompatible, and hydrophilic matrices, such as JF-based nanofibers, for preserving enzyme integrity during storage. Unlike some rigid or hydrophobic supports in previous studies, our JF-integrated electrospun system offers a highly hydrated microenvironment, which may better mimic natural aqueous conditions and contribute to long-term enzymatic preservation.

The kinetic parameters of free and immobilized laccase were determined based on classical Michaelis-Menten kinetics in order to evaluate the impact of immobilization on enzyme substrate affinity and catalytic efficiency (Table 4 ). As expected, immobilization led to an increase in K m values and a decrease in V max values, consistent with trends commonly observed for immobilized enzyme systems. The K m value for the free laccase was determined to be 0.42 ± 0.022 mM, indicating high substrate affinity under the given conditions. Upon immobilization, the K m increased to 0.76 ± 0.018 mM for PVA, 0.63 ± 0.031 mM for PVA/JF5, and 0.57 ± 0.029 mM for PVA/JF25. This moderate increase reflects a slight reduction in substrate affinity, likely resulting from diffusion limitations and possible conformational restrictions imposed by the immobilization matrix. It should also be noted that the porosity and surface area values reported in Table 2 were obtained prior to enzyme immobilization. The actual effective porosity and surface exposure during catalysis may be significantly altered due to enzyme deposition, coverage, or partial pore blockage, which could contribute to the observed differences in kinetic parameters. Notably, the lowest K m among the immobilized forms was observed for the PVA/JF25, suggesting that the JF-based nanofiber matrix provided a more favorable microenvironment that reduced mass transfer resistance and better preserved the enzyme's substrate binding ability. Similarly, immobilization resulted in a modest decrease in V max. The free laccase exhibited a maximum reaction velocity of 0.96 ± 0.044 mmol/L × min, while the corresponding value for PVA/JF25 immobilized laccase was 0.72 ± 0.038 mmol/L × min. This reduction is commonly attributed to the restricted mobility of immobilized enzymes and limited substrate accessibility. However, the relatively high V max retained by the PVA/JF25 supported laccase indicates that the structural and physicochemical features of the JF-based support effectively mitigated the adverse effects of immobilization on catalytic turnover. These kinetic results confirm that while immobilization slightly affects the catalytic parameters, the use of JF-based nanofibers enables the preservation of high enzymatic performance. Similar observations namely increased K m and decreased V max have been reported in other laccase immobilization studies as well [77,81,85,88].

To enable a valid comparison of the catalytic performance of the different immobilized enzyme systems, all BPA degradation experiments were conducted under standardized reaction conditions (pH 4.5 and 35 °C), which represent the optimal activity profile of free laccase. This uniform experimental design eliminates variability arising from differing pH or temperature effects and enables a fair benchmarking of each immobilized catalyst's efficiency.

Fig. 10 illustrates the time-dependent degradation performance of free laccase and the three immobilized enzyme systems: PVA, PVA/JF5, and PVA/JF25. The free enzyme removed approximately 46 % of BPA within the first 75 min, after which its catalytic activity plateaued. In contrast, all immobilized systems demonstrated enhanced and prolonged degradation performance. Among them, PVA/JF25 nanofibers exhibited the highest activity, achieving complete BPA removal (100 %) within 120 min. The PVA/JF5 and PVA supports also improved BPA degradation compared to the free enzyme, reaching 73.42 % and 62.32 % removal, respectively. These improvements can be attributed to increased enzyme stability, reduced diffusional limitations, and favorable microenvironments provided by the nanofiber matrices. The superior performance of PVA/JF25 likely stems from enhanced porosity, higher surface area, and the presence of functional groups in the JF biopolymer that facilitate more effective enzyme immobilization and mass transfer.

To assess substrate tolerance, Fig. 11a shows the degradation efficiency of all systems at varying initial BPA concentrations (5, 10, 20, and 40 mg L−1). While all enzyme forms achieved complete removal at 5 mg L−1, performance differences became pronounced at higher concentrations. The free enzyme exhibited a sharp decline in efficiency, removing only 75 %, 50 %, and 18 % of BPA at 10, 20, and 40 mg L−1, respectively. In contrast, PVA/JF25 consistently outperformed other systems, maintaining 100 % removal at 5, 10, and 20 mg L−1, and 66 % at 40 mg L−1. The PVA/JF5 and PVA nanofibers also demonstrated better tolerance than the free enzyme, though with some decline at 40 mg L−1. These results suggest that the nanofiber supports, particularly PVA/JF25, mitigate substrate inhibition effects and support higher catalytic loads by facilitating mass transfer and stabilizing the enzyme.

The operational reusability of the immobilized systems was evaluated over ten successive degradation cycles (Fig. 11b). While all systems showed gradual activity loss, the PVA/JF25 nanofiber again demonstrated the most robust performance, retaining 52 % of its initial activity after 10 cycles. In comparison, PVA/JF5 and PVA retained 24 % and 9 %, respectively. The enhanced stability of PVA/JF25 may be attributed to stronger enzyme-support interactions, reduced enzyme leaching, and resistance to structural deformation during repetitive use. These findings reinforce the suitability of PVA/JF25 as a highly effective and durable immobilization matrix for environmental biocatalysis applications.

Collectively, the results indicate that enzyme immobilization on JF-enriched PVA nanofibers especially PVA/JF25 significantly enhances BPA degradation efficiency, substrate tolerance, and reusability under standardized conditions. The comparative data acquired under consistent immobilization and reaction parameters provide a reliable assessment of the intrinsic catalytic performance of each formulation, addressing previous concerns regarding variability in experimental design.

This study successfully demonstrates the fabrication and application of JF-NanoMats as novel biopolymeric platforms for enzyme immobilization. By blending PVA with JF extract and optimizing electrospinning parameters, structurally stable and highly porous nanofibers were developed. Among the formulations, PVA/JF25 emerged as the most effective support, offering superior enzyme loading capacity, thermal resistance, and operational reusability. Immobilized laccase retained high catalytic performance under varying pH and temperature conditions, and effectively degraded BPA across a range of concentrations. The improved storage stability and recyclability of the JF-NanoMat based systems further emphasize their applicability in practical wastewater treatment processes, for example in batch or continuous-flow bioreactors, or as functional layers in hybrid membrane-biocatalyst systems for industrial effluents. Overall, this work not only introduces a marine-derived material into the field of enzyme immobilization but also provides a sustainable and efficient strategy for phenolic pollutant remediation. Looking forward, future studies may explore the scalability of JF-NanoMat production, integration into pilot-scale wastewater treatment plants, and applicability to other classes of emerging contaminants such as pharmaceuticals and pesticides. Moreover, coupling with multi-enzyme systems or advanced membrane processes may open further opportunities for developing robust, high-performance, and eco-friendly water purification technologies.
